title: Epistolae
author: Sidonius Apollinaris
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0261.stoa002.opp-lat6, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Non nequiter te concilii tempore, post sedentes censentesque juvenes, inglorium rusticum, senem stantem, nobilem latitabundum pauperis honorati sententia premet, cum eos quos esset indignum si vestigia nostra sequerentur, videris dolens antecessisse. Sed quid plura? Si pateris hortantem conatuum tuorum socius adjutor, praevius particeps ero. Sin autem illecebrosis deliciarum cassibus involutus, mavis, ut aiunt, Epicuri dogmatibus copulari, qui jactura virtutis admissa, summum 15 bonum sola corporis voluptate determinat, testor ecce majores, testor posteros nostros, huic me noxæ non esse confinem.
passages.english: It will weigh on you, and not undeservedly, at the time of the council, when, after young men seated and voting, after an undistinguished rustic, after an old man standing, you, a nobleman lying in hiding, are pressed down by the opinion of a poor man who has been honoured, when you see with grief that those who would have been unworthy even to follow in our footsteps have gone ahead of you. But why say more? If you allow me to urge you on, I will be the companion of your efforts, your helper, your guide, your partner. But if, entangled in the alluring snares of pleasures, you prefer, as they say, to be joined to the doctrines of Epicurus, who, once the loss of virtue has been accepted, defines the highest good by bodily pleasure alone, look, I call our ancestors to witness, I call our descendants to witness, that I have no share in this fault.
passages.notes: '15' in the text is a page or line number from the printed edition and is omitted. The first sentence is compressed and its construction is uncertain. It seems to describe the order of precedence in the council, in which the noble addressee would rank below young men, a rustic, an old man and a poor man who has been honoured.

passages.original: Et vere intra Eusebianos lares talium te quædam moneta susceperat disciplinarum, cujus philoso- phica incude formatus: nunc varias nobis rerum sermonumque rationes, ipso etiam qui docuerat, probante paudebas : nunc ut Plato discipulus jam propre potior sub Socrate, sic jam tu sub Eusebio nostro, inter Aristotelicas categorias artifex dialecticus atticissabas, cum ille adhuc ætatulam nostram, mobi. lem, teneram, crudam, modo castigatoria severitate decoqueret, modo 86 mandatorum salubritate condiret.
passages.english: And truly, within the household of Eusebius a kind of mint for such disciplines had received you, and you were shaped on its philosophical anvil. At one moment you were laying out for us various accounts of things and of speech, with the approval even of the man who had taught [you]. At another, just as Plato, a pupil, was already almost the superior under Socrates, so you now, under our Eusebius, a skilled dialectician among the Aristotelian categories, were speaking like an Athenian. Meanwhile he was still now refining our tender age, restless, soft and raw, with corrective severity, now seasoning it with the wholesomeness of his precepts.
passages.notes: 'paudebas' is read as 'pandebas' (you laid out), 'propre' as 'prope', and 'mobi. lem' as 'mobilem'. '86' is a page number from the printed edition and is omitted.

passages.original: teque per Gallias uno magistro 214 sub hac tempestate bellorum Latina tenuerunt ora portura cum pertulerint arma naufragium. Debent igitur vel æquævi, vel posteri nostri, universatim ferventibus votis alterum te ut Demosthenem, alterum ut Tu!lium, nunc statuis, si liceat, consecrare, nunc imaginibus : qui te docente formati institutique jam sinu in medio sic gentis invictæ, quod tamen alienæ, talium vetustorum signa retinebunt.
passages.english: and through you, a single teacher, throughout the Gauls in this time of wars, Latin speech has held to its harbour, though arms have suffered shipwreck. Therefore our contemporaries, or our descendants, ought all together, with fervent prayers, to consecrate you as a second Demosthenes, a second Tully [Cicero], now with statues, if it were permitted, now with portraits. For those who have been formed and trained by your teaching, though now in the very lap of an unconquered but foreign people, will keep the marks of such ancient [men].
passages.notes: The passage begins in mid-sentence. 'portura' is read as 'portum' (harbour). '214' is a page number from the printed edition and is omitted. The final clause is obscure and its sense is uncertain.

passages.original: Cum primum- Durdegalam veni, litteras mihi tabellarius tuus obtulit plenas nectaris, florum, margaritarum : quibus silentium meum culpas, et aliquos versuum meorum versibus poscis, qui tibi solent per musicum palati concavum, variata voce tinnientes, quasi libiis multiforatilibus effundi. Sed hoc tu mu- nificentia regis satis abutens, jam securus post munera facis : quia forsitan satyricum illud de satyrico non recordaris; Satur est, cum dicit Horatius evoe. Quid multa? Merito me cantare ex otio jubes, quia te jam saltare delectat. Quidquid illud est, pareo tamen; idque non modo non coactus, verum etiam spontaliter facio. Tantum tu utcunque moderere Cato- nianum superciliosae frontis arbitrium.' Nosti eniiu prope laetitiam poetarum : quorum sic ingenia mœroribus, ut pisciculi retibus amiciuntur : et si quid asperum aut trisie, non statim se poetica teneritudo a vinculo incursi angoris elaqueat.
passages.english: As soon as I came to Bordeaux, your letter-carrier handed me a letter full of nectar, flowers and pearls. In it you blame my silence and demand some verses of mine in return for your verses, which tend to pour out of you through the musical hollow of your palate, ringing with varied voice as if from many-holed pipes. But you, making ample use of the king's generosity, do this already free from care, after your rewards, because perhaps you do not remember that satirical remark about a satirist: 'Horace is well fed when he cries "evoe".' Why say more? You rightly order me to sing out of leisure, because you now delight in dancing. Whatever it is, I obey all the same, and I do it not only without compulsion but even of my own accord. Only you should in some way moderate the Catonian judgement of your haughty brow. For you know well the gladness of poets: their talents are caught by sorrows as little fish are by nets, and if there is anything harsh or sad, poetic tenderness does not at once free itself from the bond of the anxiety that has befallen it.
passages.notes: 'libiis' is read as 'tibiis' (pipes), and 'eniiu' as 'enim'. 'Nosti ... prope laetitiam' is odd; the reading may be corrupt. The quotation is Juvenal 7.62. 'Spontaliter' is a rare word meaning 'of one's own accord'.
